title: CLO 2024 Academic Month: 3D Clothing Tools and Apparel Category Design Concepts
description: Review of CLO Academic Month 2024! An interview with Mr. Yang Yi, Modeling Supervisor of the Digital Team at Jiangsu Shuntian Co., Ltd., who discussed the company’s digital transformation in the apparel industry and the more comprehensive skill requirements for designers. When designers possess design skills, pattern knowledge, and CLO software expertise simultaneously, they can better assist the apparel industry in developing more efficiently and sustainably through digital workflows. Additionally, this new type of triple-skilled talent has better career prospects. Furthermore, Mr. Yang introduced, from the perspective of a commercial designer, the customer group needs that must be considered in design, helping 3D designers in the apparel industry to learn and grow.
transcript:
Hello, everyone. I am Yang Yi from Shuntian Group, Jiangsu Province.  
I am currently working on the 3D digitalization of clothing.  
Today, I would like to share with you the concept of 3D clothing tools and clothing design.  
As you all know, the digital wave has already swept across various industries, including our clothing industry.  
For example, the CROA 4-core that we used before, and the AI tools that will appear in the future, are all part of our digitalization process.  
Creating new technologies and using new technologies is inevitable for human progress.  
The digital wave from 3D to 2D virtual reality is emerging in various fields.  
From the development of design to the end of sales, the clothing industry is evolving towards 3D digitalization.  
The fashion industry is evolving towards 3D digitalization.  
Currently, most of the development in our company is based on digitalized tools.  
It can reduce the cost of materials and human resources, and at the same time shorten the release cycle of our products, increase system efficiency, and improve the acceptance rate of our clothing.  
Some companies abroad, such as Google and Amazon, are also actively developing AI designers.  
They want to use fashion trend reports, trend data, image analysis, and so on, to create AI designers.  
Although currently these tools and software may only assist designers, I believe that after global updates, they will make a huge contribution to the fashion industry.  
At the same time, we can also use AIGC technology to match different clothing design styles and make individualized predictions to help the fashion industry judge product quality.  
For example, the American fashion brand Tommy recently announced cooperation with IBM and the New York Fashion Institute (FIT) to use IBM's technology for fashion decoding.  
AIGC, as the current new content, has been widely applied in many industries, including smart offices, technology education, automated production, smart medicine, and of course, our clothing industry.  
Currently, our company’s use of AIGC involves three processes: planning, design and development, and product marketing.  

In the planning phase, we may use big data from the Internet or trend data to carry out trend analysis, including color trends, industry trends, design trends, etc., which then guide our development process.  
In the development process, we use trends from the planning phase to carry out design, which may lead to unexpected trends.  
Finally, when these trends go online or are sold on the Internet, we use AIGC technology to produce online videos or sales content.  
These applications rely on our software tools, and we can use AIGC technology to produce online content.  

Here, I have compiled some of the software we currently use.  
Some are familiar to you, such as MD, Clo, Stealth 3D, ET, Blender, and so on.  
There are also some newly popular ones, such as Mid Journey, Stable Diffusion, etc.  
There may also be some you have not seen before or logos you’ve seen less often, such as Spiral, Houdini, 3D Max, and Maya.  

In recent years, we have been designing clothes using traditional design software such as AIPS or Procreate used on tablets.  
However, in the past two years, all our clothing design software has undergone a series of revisions.  
We have used ET, Fuyi, and CAD software for clothing design.  
For example, we used CCD, Blender, 3D Max, or Maya to design clothing models, accessories, and modeling.  
We have also used Pixblend, AI, and Photoshop to design fabrics and prints.  
Finally, we have used MD, Clo, Stealth 3D, and Blozeville for 3D clothing design software to design clothes digitally.  
In Intel, we have used MD, Clo, NGC, and STABL.  
Finally, we used 3D Max, Maya, and other software for environment design.  
We used Mid Journey and Stable Diffusion for environment design.  
Finally, we used CCD, Blender, and Houdini for fabric pattern design.  

On the right, you can see a recent project we collaborated on.  
One of the requirements was to create a thin, airy, and cool design for a sun visor.  
When modeling, we chose relatively thin fabric to create a semi-thin effect.  
In Maya and 3D Max, we created an icy background and added strong sunlight.  
Finally, in Blender and Houdini, we simulated the thinness of the floating fabric and completed a series of visual designs.  
This is the presentation of the costume’s digital selling point.  

But can our process really achieve such an effect?  
A few days ago, a friend asked me: after your company uses these digital software tools, have you calculated how much cost you save or how much you speed up your company’s efficiency or progress?  
So I reflected.  
I compared some of the time we spent developing designs and the selection rate of our designs.  
After comparison, I found that if we use the traditional way of thinking with 3D, which is to draw an effect picture, create a 3D version, simulate it with Clo, and then sew the costume, what did we find?  
Before using 3D, maybe in 2017 or 2018, our designer drew a design, which might take half a day. Then it took a day to create a 3D version in the studio.  
After half a day of training, the designer gave us a sample, and then the board was modified.  
After confirmation, it might take another two days to line up, and finally, the actual sample was completed.  
This process took about 14 days, almost half a month.  

After we started using 3D software in 2019, our designer still needed half a day to draw a picture and a day to create the board.  
Then we lined it up for a day.  
The only change is that we now use Clo 3D for special simulation, which might take from half a day to two hours.  
But the cost of the 3D model and the sample is similar, not much different.  
It might take more than two hours, then the designer gives feedback, and the board is modified again.  
After confirmation, we still need two more days to make a sample.  
It is clearly digitalized and a one-time modification.  
It used to take 14 working days, but now it still takes 13.5 working days to make a sample.  
Our efficiency may have improved slightly, but the designer’s monthly production may have decreased.  
Our model may also need fine-tuning before it can be promoted, as I mentioned earlier.  
We calculated carefully, and it seems there is no significant change.  

Then we designed a process where the designer simulates rather than creates.  
Let the designer simulate with a 3D modeling machine.  
Our 3D modeling machine can do more professional tasks, such as client designs or long-term modeling.  
This way, we can increase the time and efficiency of the 3D modeling machine.  
But we found that if we use this process, the designer’s design style time will also be reduced, causing issues.  
At the same time, it may still take more than ten days.  
There is no change, which greatly reduces our design or simulation cycle.  

Assuming there is no intermediate environment, if the designer does not know how to model, and designs a 3D model by himself, then the model is modeled according to his 3D model, after which the designer simulates it, finally completing the design simulation, this cycle will be shortened by half — almost from the first cycle to the second cycle.  
In this way, the model is simulated.  

If the designer knows how to model a 3D model, for example, a designer familiar with 3D modeling, even if he spends one or two days building a model in Clo 3D or other familiar 3D software, he can adjust it to the desired model.  
He only needs to queue for one day and go to the simulation center, which may take one to three days.  
This way, the model can be simulated very quickly.  

After a series of experiments, because most designers do not know how to model, we chose to conduct experiments in the first cycle.  
Indeed, some designers can produce two to three or even three to four samples a week.  
Currently, the speed is quite fast.  
There is a designer in our company who knows how to model 3D and may produce a sample in four to five days.  

This is a video of us designing a 3D model directly through digital tools.  
I don’t know if you can see it.  
Mr. Yang just said he can’t see the video.  
Anna, can we see the video?  
Yes, we can.  
Okay.  

Now we are doing a simple board operation in this Pro software.  
There is a timer below.  
Okay.  
This is a simple timer I made two days ago.  
It takes about five minutes to make a 3D model, then about five minutes to simulate it.  
It takes about ten minutes to complete a simple modeling process including hardware design, action, and material confirmation.  
After that, it takes about ten minutes to complete a 3D model.  
This model is relatively simple.  
If it is a raincoat, jacket, or shirt, it may take about half an hour to an hour.  
This also depends on our designer’s familiarity with the model.  

In this mode, the model and the board become secondary products.  
When our design draft comes out, you don’t need to make additional designs.  
You can have our model and the board, which shortens the sample production period.  
Because in our Pro software, the board can directly output DXF to our ET system or connect directly to our printer to print the board and send it to our sample room.  

But at the same time, we have encountered a difficulty.  
Many friends ask, if I don’t know how to make a board, how should I design?  
Because many designers are not from professional modeling classes.  
They may like this industry, or love clothing or fashion, then start learning how to design or switch to another field.  
Designers with professional backgrounds or college education basically understand some modeling, but their understanding is not deep enough.  
So how should they start designing?  
Some people think design efficiency will decrease.  
They used to spend a long time on design style, but now they may spend much energy making a board.  
It takes a long time building a board from scratch.  
Some say they can’t let go of traditional methods; they can design naturally with lines but now struggle with software.  

So I want to talk about today’s topic.  
If you want to solve these problems, you need to understand a logic: choose the design logic based on categories.  
That is, the design philosophy of clothing categories in the digital age.  

Speaking of categories, consider this question: what is the relationship between the suit category and the clothing category?  
For example, at the company annual meeting, everyone is told to wear a suit.  
But the same colleagues may choose casual clothes for team building.  
In our mind, categories may be related to scenes and applications.  
Thus, needs are categorized.  

To extend this idea, needs are divided into categories.  
Because our design purpose is to solve problems and meet needs.  
I found two pictures: one is a team-building scene, the other an annual meeting scene.  
The same group may wear different clothes in different scenes, but within the same category, there may be different choices for different scenes.  

For example, in the suit category:  
The suit worn at a wedding, the groom’s suit, the guest’s suit, or the suit worn in the company office meeting must differ.  
This is the division of needs and categories.  

Starting from categories, the design criterion is mainly based on people’s needs, satisfying the needs of specific people for different clothes in different situations.  
These needs include beauty, professionalism, flexibility, empathy, and comfort.  

From people research, we identify product divisions — this is the first step of our design thinking.  
This is a case of people analysis.  
Market analysis involves many divisions; here, I give a division of people analysis from four aspects: geographical, community, psychological, and behavioral.  

After people analysis, we get a “medical life plan.”  
Some of you may be unfamiliar with this term.  
A medical life plan means what clothes you wear daily or weekly.  
Imagine when you wake up every morning, the first thing you think about is what to wear.  
You open your closet and choose what to wear.  
For example, if I have an important meeting this morning, I may choose a shirt plus a suit.  
If I want to go hiking today, I may choose outdoor clothes.  
This is my daily life plan.  

For example, if I go to work Monday to Friday, I may wear formal clothes.  
If I travel on weekends, I may wear outdoor clothes.  
This is my life plan, related to our needs in life.  

Then we have specific, detailed needs to generate detailed evaluations.  
For example, what is my personality?  
Personality, color, style, and taste — these four aspects will be designed.  

Personality is our daily life style, including color management, color ratio, color scheme, etc.  
For example, we consider the proportion of social, commuting, fashion, home, and leisure wear — for instance, 6:1:1:2 (just an example).  

Style management might be by product.  
We recorded that clothing technology accounts for 80%, fashion or trend clothes for 20%.  
This is the standard for most of our people.  

Our rating management might be by different clothing combinations: tops, bottoms, top and bottom, accessories, etc.  

Finally, in clothing design, after having the above life plan, we design specific items for the targeted people.  
For example, what patterns suit them?  
Patterns relate to the segment categories mentioned earlier.  

For example, take me: my clothing type may be more professional or casual.  
So, my segment category chooses patterns from professional and casual styles.  
For example, the jacket I’m wearing today is more outdoor.  
Its pattern is an outdoor pattern.  

Regarding craftsmanship, it combines traditional and new techniques.  
For example, this windbreaker may use ordinary craftsmanship such as pressurized or waterproof fabric technology, lacing, zipper structure sewing, etc.  
On this dress, for example, the screen printing and laser engraving are new craftsmanship.  
Traditional and new craftsmanship combine on this dress.  

Fabric selection is also a combination of traditional fabric and popular fashion.  
For example, this dress uses traditional nylon fabric combined with popular cliquette fabric in a three-in-one fabric.  
Inside the fabric combination is a super-thin maza fabric, the latest waterproof and breathable 10K/10K fabric.  
It is very different fabric.  

This dress suits different scenarios: it can be worn on rainy days, in cold mountain weather, or in the office — providing multiple functions.  

Regarding materials, we define them as solving problems.  
For example, a molding pad solves a sleeve problem, the zipper solves opening-closing problems, etc.  

Finally, color mainly relates to trends and functional colors.  
Most people like black, which is also a functional color reflecting needs of those who don’t like to show off.  
Such needs are internal needs that the design satisfies.  

This is an example of how outdoor products become a trend.  
For example, Xiao Wang likes outdoor sports and visits Dahao and Shenzhen during free time.  
He needs equipment like a windscreen catcher, headlamp, and cover.  

Our windscreen catcher category has many types: pressure-trim, non-pressure-trim, three-in-one windscreen catchers, etc.  
There are six types in our country.  
The example here is a three-in-one windscreen catcher.  
The recommended product is a standard three-in-one windbreaker with a braided version.  
It requires flat workmanship, pressurization, and being two-in-one (removable).  

For fabric, we choose waterproof, composite, functional braided fabric.  
Accessories include chain, magic sticker, spring-loaded collar, etc.  
Colors include common men's clothing colors such as turquoise, green, black, and gray, and currently popular colors.  

Once we decide on accessory categories and our one-in-one plan, our pattern will have a fixed shape.  
This solves the problem that designers may not know how to make or understand patterns.  
When making patterns, we are aware of the audience’s needs.  
Patterns become secondary products that appear naturally.  

For example, suits are often misunderstood as having no room for design or all looking the same.  
Suits are worn in certain seasons or occasions but are diverse.  

We have a variety of jacket and coat collections made from different suit patterns.  
For example, a basic suit set with a front split can make a jacket suit, sports suits, T-shirts, and black suits.  
In jacket styles, there are forest jackets, hunting jackets, advanced jackets, Norfolk jackets, etc.  
In sports suits, there are standard and professional sports suits.  
So suit design is very diverse.  

This is what I showed you: the English, American, and French versions of Tashdor.  
These are types of suits.  
Some of you may not have heard the special terms.  
But looking at design, for example, a hunting jacket has a chest pocket on the left, a three-dimensional chest jacket, or a horseback jacket — you can clearly see design differences.  

From men’s to women’s suits, they gradually evolve into different types seen today.  

We can divide standard suit patterns by collar type, such as a pimpon collar, button type (probably two-button), bottom shape (round bottom), double-sided line pockets, left chest hand strap, three-dimensional buckles, back openings, etc.  
These are all design details.  

With these details, we can start from a basic suit version to make changes and designs.  
We can design while minimizing our pattern work, then modify it.  
Modifications may focus on clothing width and basic size.  

The jacket below is inspired by a technical jacket.  
After width and size are set, shoulder shape is designed — for example, shoulder sleeves or full sleeves.  
Then seam allowance and hemline design, including chest hemline in women’s suits and shoulder hemline in men’s suits, are processed.  
You can add collars, split lines, or pull fleece fabric, then process the hemline and shoulder hemline.  

Fourth is the leader design.  
Leader design determines the clothes’ appearance.  
This is my personal view.  
Leaders in our culture, like spiritual or team leaders, are important positions.  
Hence the term “leader.”  
In clothing, collar design (including hats) and sleeve design determine whether clothes look good.  
Collar design may involve two-piece sleeves, suit sleeves, or shirt sleeves.  

Fifth are internal structures.  
For example, whether to have inside pockets, press collars inside, or design two-piece suits inside.  
These are considerations about internal structures.  

Lastly, part design includes decorative parts such as logos or decorative zippers.  
These do not greatly impact overall clothing or function but affect appearance.  
Parts design also plays a role in collar design.  

After these steps, the 3D model of our suit is completed.  
When you consider the type of people, distribution, life plan, pattern characteristics, and so on, you have basically completed this design series.  
Then you select the correct fabric from your fabric warehouse and make fabric support.  

This is what I described through product type thinking: what product type to choose, what people to target, what distribution to apply, and design accordingly.  
This is just one of many design trends.  
For example, we have a trend website and design trends that have slightly changed from previous flagships.  
However, all design trends have technical aspects.  

For example, in college, I learned design from style and style trends.  
It captures current fashion selling points and makes extensions.  
So, what I accept now is that the 3D design we use is actually the most suitable design based on product category.  

Okay.  

Finally, I want to talk about the future of 3D fashion designers.  
Recently, I have some self-media accounts.  
I learned a lot about 3D fashion.  
Many universities started digital fashion programs in 2021 or 2022.  
They are now facing graduation and employment issues.  
Many students have added me on WeChat.  
They ask what I see in the future, whether to work in fashion or digitalization, such as 3D model designers, animation artists, special effects artists, etc.  
They don’t know what to do.  
Some worry about future employment.  

So, I want to share my views on the future of this industry.  

I list three directions:  
1. Brands of small and exquisite designers.  
2. Brands of 3-in-1 designers — those who can do digitalization and design.  
3. Golden partners of fashion artists — fashion business owners in trade companies working with designers to solve customer problems, especially technical solutions online.  

What are the three directions?  
- Small and exquisite designer brands.  
- Big designer brands, possibly large companies but not necessarily state-owned.  
- Trade companies, usually state-owned.  

These are three major directions for designers.  
However, in the future, designers in these companies may need to go through a small stage and upgrade, or may be eliminated.  
Future designers may enter these companies and bring new motivation.  

Let me give an example of a 3-in-1 designer.  
Many designers in our company know how to build 3D models.  
However, some new designers, such as recent graduates or those from other companies, find their design style, choice rate, or completion level is worse compared to designers proficient in 3D modeling.  

Another example: when some of our clothing businessmen meet brands, the brand often raises tricky questions.  
Some businessmen call or video conference designers or technical guides to get online answers.  
Designers who know 3D modeling may bring a computer to meet clients and solve 3D model, fabric, and hardware problems one-on-one.  
Clients highly appreciate this efficient problem-solving process that focuses on key points immediately.  

In comparison, designers who don’t know 3D modeling may have similar tasks but are less efficient.  
Designers knowing 3D modeling will be more involved in the core of clients or brands.  

So, I think 3D design is not just about modeling; it is a new skill, a new capability in our profession.  

Finally, I want to say digital automation is a big trend in business.  
For fashion companies, optimizing future strategy, streamlining processes, product delivery, customer upgrades, and business model innovation are all driven by data.  

Therefore, the fashion industry should accelerate and enhance digital transformation and open new business methods and communication channels.  

Thank you, everyone. I have finished my sharing.

chunks.content: ## Introduction to 3D Clothing Tools and Apparel Category Design Concepts This section introduces the digital transformation in the clothing industry, focusing on 3D clothing tools, AI technologies, and the integration of digitalization throughout the fashion supply chain. Key concepts include 3D digitalization, AI-assisted design, and AIGC (Artificial Intelligence Generated Content) applications. The clothing industry is rapidly evolving through digitalization, moving from traditional 2D design to immersive 3D virtual reality tools. Technologies like Clo 3D, MD, and AI tools are becoming essential in reducing material and labor costs, shortening product release cycles, and improving design acceptance rates. Global tech companies such as Google and Amazon are also developing AI designers that leverage fashion trend reports, image analysis, and big data to assist or even lead design processes. AIGC technology is applied in three main phases within the industry: - **Planning:** Utilizing internet-sourced big data and trend analysis (color, design, industry trends) to guide product development. - **Design and Development:** Executing designs informed by trend data, allowing for innovative or unexpected trends to emerge. - **Product Marketing:** Creating online videos and sales content using AI-generated media to enhance product visibility. Software tools commonly used include Clo, MD, Stealth 3D, ET, Blender, Mid Journey, Stable Diffusion, Spiral, Houdini, 3D Max, and Maya. These tools cover a range of functions from fabric and print design to 3D modeling and environmental rendering. --- ## Software Tools and Digital Design Workflow in 3D Apparel Development This section details the software ecosystem used for 3D clothing design, modeling, fabric texture creation, and environmental simulation. It also explores the evolution of design workflows and efficiencies gained through digital tools. Traditionally, apparel design utilized software like AIPS and Procreate on tablets. Recently, the industry expanded to include CAD systems, ET, Fuyi, and specialized 3D modeling software such as Blender, 3D Max, Maya, Pixblend, AI tools, and Photoshop for fabrics and prints. For 3D clothing simulation, MD, Clo, Stealth 3D, and Blozeville are prominent. Environment design is handled with Mid Journey, Stable Diffusion, and Houdini. A case study highlights a project involving a sun visor designed with thin, airy fabric simulated in Maya, 3D Max, Blender, and Houdini. These tools allowed realistic simulation of fabric thinness and visual effects like icy backgrounds and strong sunlight, aiding digital selling points. --- ## Evaluation of Efficiency and Cost Savings Using 3D Digitalization This section analyzes the impact of adopting 3D digital tools on design cycle times, cost savings, and productivity within clothing development. Pre-2019, the design-to-sample cycle took approximately 14 working days, involving manual drawing, 3D version creation, sample preparation, and modifications. After adopting Clo 3D and related software in 2019, the cycle reduced marginally to about 13.5 days, with simulations replacing some manual steps, but overall sample production time remained similar. Alternative workflows involve designers focusing on simulation rather than modeling, delegating modeling to specialized 3D teams, or having designers skilled in both modeling and simulation.

chunks.content: --- ## Evaluation of Efficiency and Cost Savings Using 3D Digitalization This section analyzes the impact of adopting 3D digital tools on design cycle times, cost savings, and productivity within clothing development. Pre-2019, the design-to-sample cycle took approximately 14 working days, involving manual drawing, 3D version creation, sample preparation, and modifications. After adopting Clo 3D and related software in 2019, the cycle reduced marginally to about 13.5 days, with simulations replacing some manual steps, but overall sample production time remained similar. Alternative workflows involve designers focusing on simulation rather than modeling, delegating modeling to specialized 3D teams, or having designers skilled in both modeling and simulation. Designers proficient in 3D modeling can reduce sample production to 4-5 days by building and adjusting models directly in Clo 3D and simulating them efficiently. A practical demonstration showed that simple 3D models could be created and simulated within 10 minutes, while more complex garments like raincoats or jackets might require 30 minutes to an hour, depending on designer proficiency. --- ## Pro Software Integration and Digital Board Production This section explains the integration of Pro software in the digital design process, streamlining pattern making and sample production through DXF output and direct printing. In the digital workflow, the design draft produces both a 3D model and a board (pattern), which can be directly output as DXF files to ET systems or printers, facilitating quick pattern printing and sample room delivery. This reduces the need for separate manual pattern making, shortening sample production time. Challenges remain for designers unfamiliar with board making or 3D modeling, especially those with non-technical or non-professional modeling backgrounds. Such designers may struggle with software proficiency, increasing design time or reducing style output. --- ## Design Logic Based on Apparel Categories and User Needs This section discusses the importance of categorizing clothing designs based on user needs, scenarios, and product categories to improve design efficiency and relevancy. Design categories relate to context and application, such as suits for formal events versus casual wear for team building. Within categories, designs can vary significantly based on occasions—for example, wedding suits differ from office suits. Design philosophy prioritizes meeting specific user needs like aesthetics, professionalism, flexibility, empathy, and comfort. People analysis divides target users into geographical, community, psychological, and behavioral segments to tailor designs effectively. A "medical life plan" concept illustrates daily clothing decisions based on lifestyle, such as formal wear for workdays and outdoor wear for weekends. Detailed evaluations consider personality, color preferences, style, and taste to refine design direction. --- ## Pattern, Craftsmanship, and Material Selection in Apparel Design This section outlines the integration of traditional and innovative craftsmanship, fabric selection, and material functionality in digital clothing design. Patterns are derived based on targeted user segments and lifestyle needs. Craftsmanship combines traditional techniques like pressurized waterproof fabric technology, lacing, and zipper sewing, with modern methods such as screen printing and laser engraving.

chunks.content: Detailed evaluations consider personality, color preferences, style, and taste to refine design direction. --- ## Pattern, Craftsmanship, and Material Selection in Apparel Design This section outlines the integration of traditional and innovative craftsmanship, fabric selection, and material functionality in digital clothing design. Patterns are derived based on targeted user segments and lifestyle needs. Craftsmanship combines traditional techniques like pressurized waterproof fabric technology, lacing, and zipper sewing, with modern methods such as screen printing and laser engraving. Fabric choices blend traditional materials (e.g., nylon) with fashionable, functional composites like three-in-one fabrics featuring super-thin maza layers and waterproof, breathable 10K/10K technology, enabling multi-functional garments suitable for various weather and environments. Material components are selected to solve specific functional problems, such as molding pads for sleeve shaping or zippers for closures. Color selection balances trend-driven and functional colors, with black often preferred for its understated appeal. --- ## Case Study: Outdoor Apparel and Accessory Design This section presents an example of outdoor product design, focusing on windscreen catchers and windbreakers with detailed accessory and fabric choices. The windscreen catcher category includes six types domestically, including pressure-trim, non-pressure-trim, and three-in-one types. The recommended product is a standard three-in-one windbreaker with braided fabric, requiring flat workmanship, pressurization, and two-in-one (detachable) functionality. Fabric selection favors waterproof, composite, functional braided textiles. Accessories include chains, magic stickers (Velcro), spring-loaded collars, and more. Color palettes incorporate popular men's clothing colors such as turquoise, green, black, and gray, alongside trending hues. Establishing accessory and pattern categories fixes pattern shapes, helping designers unfamiliar with pattern making to deliver consistent, need-based designs. --- ## Suit Design Diversity and Technical Details This section explores the variety within suit design, emphasizing that suits are diverse by season, occasion, and style rather than uniform. Suit collections include various jacket and coat styles, such as forest jackets, hunting jackets, Norfolk jackets, and sports suits with standard and professional variants. These derive from basic suit patterns modified by collar types (e.g., pimpon collar), button configurations (commonly two-button), pocket styles, and tailoring details like split lines and three-dimensional buckles. Designers can start with a basic suit template and apply modifications focusing on garment width, size, shoulder shape (shoulder sleeves vs. full sleeves), seam allowances, and hemlines tailored for gender-specific fits. Leader design emphasizes outer appearance elements like collars and sleeves, which significantly impact garment aesthetics. Internal structural design considers pockets, press collars, and lining techniques. Decorative parts such as logos and zippers contribute to appearance without major functional impact but influence overall style. --- ## Product Type Thinking and Design Trends in 3D Apparel This section explains how product type selection, target audience, distribution strategy, and fabric sourcing guide 3D clothing design and trend development. markdown_content: ## Introduction to 3D Clothing Tools and Apparel Category Design Concepts This section introduces the digital transformation in the clothing industry, focusing on 3D clothing tools, AI technologies, and the integration of digitalization throughout the fashion supply chain. Key concepts include 3D digitalization, AI-assisted design, and AIGC (Artificial Intelligence Generated Content) applications. The clothing industry is rapidly evolving through digitalization, moving from traditional 2D design to immersive 3D virtual reality tools. Technologies like Clo 3D, MD, and AI tools are becoming essential in reducing material and labor costs, shortening product release cycles, and improving design acceptance rates. Global tech companies such as Google and Amazon are also developing AI designers that leverage fashion trend reports, image analysis, and big data to assist or even lead design processes. AIGC technology is applied in three main phases within the industry: - **Planning:** Utilizing internet-sourced big data and trend analysis (color, design, industry trends) to guide product development. - **Design and Development:** Executing designs informed by trend data, allowing for innovative or unexpected trends to emerge. - **Product Marketing:** Creating online videos and sales content using AI-generated media to enhance product visibility. Software tools commonly used include Clo, MD, Stealth 3D, ET, Blender, Mid Journey, Stable Diffusion, Spiral, Houdini, 3D Max, and Maya. These tools cover a range of functions from fabric and print design to 3D modeling and environmental rendering. --- ## Software Tools and Digital Design Workflow in 3D Apparel Development This section details the software ecosystem used for 3D clothing design, modeling, fabric texture creation, and environmental simulation. It also explores the evolution of design workflows and efficiencies gained through digital tools. Traditionally, apparel design utilized software like AIPS and Procreate on tablets. Recently, the industry expanded to include CAD systems, ET, Fuyi, and specialized 3D modeling software such as Blender, 3D Max, Maya, Pixblend, AI tools, and Photoshop for fabrics and prints. For 3D clothing simulation, MD, Clo, Stealth 3D, and Blozeville are prominent. Environment design is handled with Mid Journey, Stable Diffusion, and Houdini. A case study highlights a project involving a sun visor designed with thin, airy fabric simulated in Maya, 3D Max, Blender, and Houdini. These tools allowed realistic simulation of fabric thinness and visual effects like icy backgrounds and strong sunlight, aiding digital selling points. --- ## Evaluation of Efficiency and Cost Savings Using 3D Digitalization This section analyzes the impact of adopting 3D digital tools on design cycle times, cost savings, and productivity within clothing development. Pre-2019, the design-to-sample cycle took approximately 14 working days, involving manual drawing, 3D version creation, sample preparation, and modifications. After adopting Clo 3D and related software in 2019, the cycle reduced marginally to about 13.5 days, with simulations replacing some manual steps, but overall sample production time remained similar. Alternative workflows involve designers focusing on simulation rather than modeling, delegating modeling to specialized 3D teams, or having designers skilled in both modeling and simulation. Designers proficient in 3D modeling can reduce sample production to 4-5 days by building and adjusting models directly in Clo 3D and simulating them efficiently. A practical demonstration showed that simple 3D models could be created and simulated within 10 minutes, while more complex garments like raincoats or jackets might require 30 minutes to an hour, depending on designer proficiency. --- ## Pro Software Integration and Digital Board Production This section explains the integration of Pro software in the digital design process, streamlining pattern making and sample production through DXF output and direct printing. In the digital workflow, the design draft produces both a 3D model and a board (pattern), which can be directly output as DXF files to ET systems or printers, facilitating quick pattern printing and sample room delivery. This reduces the need for separate manual pattern making, shortening sample production time. Challenges remain for designers unfamiliar with board making or 3D modeling, especially those with non-technical or non-professional modeling backgrounds. Such designers may struggle with software proficiency, increasing design time or reducing style output. --- ## Design Logic Based on Apparel Categories and User Needs This section discusses the importance of categorizing clothing designs based on user needs, scenarios, and product categories to improve design efficiency and relevancy. Design categories relate to context and application, such as suits for formal events versus casual wear for team building. Within categories, designs can vary significantly based on occasions—for example, wedding suits differ from office suits. Design philosophy prioritizes meeting specific user needs like aesthetics, professionalism, flexibility, empathy, and comfort. People analysis divides target users into geographical, community, psychological, and behavioral segments to tailor designs effectively. A "medical life plan" concept illustrates daily clothing decisions based on lifestyle, such as formal wear for workdays and outdoor wear for weekends. Detailed evaluations consider personality, color preferences, style, and taste to refine design direction. --- ## Pattern, Craftsmanship, and Material Selection in Apparel Design This section outlines the integration of traditional and innovative craftsmanship, fabric selection, and material functionality in digital clothing design. Patterns are derived based on targeted user segments and lifestyle needs. Craftsmanship combines traditional techniques like pressurized waterproof fabric technology, lacing, and zipper sewing, with modern methods such as screen printing and laser engraving. Fabric choices blend traditional materials (e.g., nylon) with fashionable, functional composites like three-in-one fabrics featuring super-thin maza layers and waterproof, breathable 10K/10K technology, enabling multi-functional garments suitable for various weather and environments. Material components are selected to solve specific functional problems, such as molding pads for sleeve shaping or zippers for closures. Color selection balances trend-driven and functional colors, with black often preferred for its understated appeal. --- ## Case Study: Outdoor Apparel and Accessory Design This section presents an example of outdoor product design, focusing on windscreen catchers and windbreakers with detailed accessory and fabric choices. The windscreen catcher category includes six types domestically, including pressure-trim, non-pressure-trim, and three-in-one types. The recommended product is a standard three-in-one windbreaker with braided fabric, requiring flat workmanship, pressurization, and two-in-one (detachable) functionality. Fabric selection favors waterproof, composite, functional braided textiles. Accessories include chains, magic stickers (Velcro), spring-loaded collars, and more. Color palettes incorporate popular men's clothing colors such as turquoise, green, black, and gray, alongside trending hues. Establishing accessory and pattern categories fixes pattern shapes, helping designers unfamiliar with pattern making to deliver consistent, need-based designs. --- ## Suit Design Diversity and Technical Details This section explores the variety within suit design, emphasizing that suits are diverse by season, occasion, and style rather than uniform. Suit collections include various jacket and coat styles, such as forest jackets, hunting jackets, Norfolk jackets, and sports suits with standard and professional variants. These derive from basic suit patterns modified by collar types (e.g., pimpon collar), button configurations (commonly two-button), pocket styles, and tailoring details like split lines and three-dimensional buckles. Designers can start with a basic suit template and apply modifications focusing on garment width, size, shoulder shape (shoulder sleeves vs. full sleeves), seam allowances, and hemlines tailored for gender-specific fits. Leader design emphasizes outer appearance elements like collars and sleeves, which significantly impact garment aesthetics. Internal structural design considers pockets, press collars, and lining techniques. Decorative parts such as logos and zippers contribute to appearance without major functional impact but influence overall style. --- ## Product Type Thinking and Design Trends in 3D Apparel This section explains how product type selection, target audience, distribution strategy, and fabric sourcing guide 3D clothing design and trend development. Small and exquisite designer brands focused on niche markets. 2. 3-in-1 designers capable of both digital modeling and traditional design. 3. Fashion business owners and technical partners in trade companies solving client problems, particularly through online technical support. Recent graduates face uncertainty regarding employment, with roles expanding beyond traditional design to include animation, special effects, and digital fashion technologies. Designers proficient in 3D modeling contribute more directly to client solutions, often collaborating via video conferences or on-site meetings, providing efficient, problem-focused service. This capability integrates designers closer to brand core operations, improving task efficiency and client satisfaction. --- ## Digital Automation and Business Model Innovation in Fashion This section emphasizes the growing role of digital automation in streamlining fashion business operations, product delivery, customer engagement, and innovation.
